entries.meaning: ‘This alone is the whole substance of royal duty, though it is concealed like a desire within the mind.’ Rāma instructed his brother in many ways, but without a tangible support Bharata's mind found neither satisfaction nor peace. Raghurāja, overcome by Bharata's character, the guru and ministers, reserve and affection, graciously gave his sandals. Bharata reverently took them and placed them upon his head. Those foot-seats of the treasury of compassion were like a pair of watchmen for the people's life, a casket for the jewel of Bharata's love, two syllables protecting living beings, the skillful doors safeguarding the dynasty's good deeds, and spotless eyes for the noble duty of service. Bharata rejoiced at gaining that support as much as if Sītā and Rāma themselves had remained. He asked leave and bowed; Rāma drew him to his breast. The people were listless, and the crooked lord of the immortals found an adverse opportunity.

entries.meaning: That crooked device proved good for everyone: hope in the appointed term became a lifeline for every heart. Otherwise, at a separation like Lakṣmaṇa's and Sītā's from Rāma, all the people would have collapsed and died from that terrible malady. Rāma's grace corrected the disorder; the appeal the gods had made became a giver of virtue. When Rāma embraced his brother Bharata with both arms, the rasa of their love cannot be told. Love surged through body, mind, and speech, and the great bearers of fortitude abandoned fortitude. The lotus-eyed brothers shed tears; seeing their condition, the assembly of gods was distressed. The bands of sages, the guru, and steadfast Janaka were like gold assayed in the fire of knowledge. Brahmā had created them detached, moving through the water of the world like lotus leaves; yet even they, seeing Raghubara's unequalled and boundless love for Bharata, were submerged in mind, body, and speech together with their detachment and reflection.

When even Janaka's and the guru's understanding was confounded, calling it ordinary affection would be a grave fault. People who hear the poet describe the separation of Raghubara and Bharata will take him for hard-hearted. That reserved rasa is ineffable; lovely Speech herself felt abashed when she remembered the occasion and the love. After embracing Bharata, Raghubara reassured him; then he joyfully drew Śatrughna, vanquisher of foes, to his heart. Servants and ministers read Bharata's inclination and each went to his task. Hearing of the dreadful grief, both royal companies began preparing every provision for departure. The two brothers bowed to the Lord's lotus feet and set out with Rāma's command upon their heads. They appealed to the sages, ascetics, and forest deities and honored each one repeatedly. After embracing Lakṣmaṇa and bowing to him, Bharata placed the dust of Sītā's feet upon his head. He departed in love, hearing blessings from all—embodiments of every auspiciousness.

Rāma and his younger brother bowed their heads to the king and honored him with many kinds of humble praise. ‘Lord, through compassion you have endured great pain and come to the forest with your entire company. Please set foot in your city and give me your blessing.’ Gathering courage, the king set out. Rāma honored sages, brahmins, and saints, regarding them as Viṣṇu and Śiva, and took leave of them. The two brothers went to their mothers, bowed at their feet, received blessings, and returned. Kauśika, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, citizens, relatives, ministers, and good servants—Rāma and his brother addressed and bowed to each as fitting and took leave of them. The treasury of compassion honored and turned back women and men, small, middle, and great. The Lord bowed at the feet of Bharata's mother, met her with pure affection, placed her in a prepared palanquin, and took leave, removing all her reserve and sorrow.

After meeting her mother, father, and relatives, Sītā returned, pure in love and dearer than life. She bowed to and embraced all her mothers-in-law; the poet's heart finds no delight in attempting to tell that love. She heard their counsel and received the blessings she desired, remaining absorbed in the love of both sides. Raghupati ordered palanquins to be brought and, after consoling all the mothers, helped them mount. Again and again the two brothers joined them with equal affection and escorted their mothers. Horses, elephants, and many kinds of vehicles were prepared, and Bharata and the king's companies set out. Carrying Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa in their hearts, all the people went like those bereft of awareness. Oxen, horses, elephants, and other animals moved with defeated hearts, compelled onward while crushing their feelings. With Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, the Lord bowed at the feet of guru and guru's wife; then they returned, filled with mingled joy and wonder, and came to their leaf-thatched home.

Rāma honored the Niṣāda king and took leave of him; Guha departed with deep anguish of separation in his heart. Kols, Kirātas, Bhillas, and other forest-dwellers were sent back, repeatedly offering reverent greetings as they returned. Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa sat beneath the banyan's shade and grieved at separation from their beloved family. Overcome by love, Rāma described Bharata's affection, nature, and gracious speech to his beloved and younger brother. He spoke from his holy mouth of Bharata's love and trust in word, thought, and deed. At that moment birds, animals, aquatic creatures, and every moving and unmoving being of Citrakūṭa grew dejected. Seeing Raghubara's condition, the gods showered flowers, reported that each company was on its way home, bowed to the Lord, and offered reassurance. They departed with glad minds, no longer deeply afraid. With Sītā and his younger brother, the Lord shone in the leaf hut like devotion, knowledge, and detachment embodied.

Sages, brahmins, guru, Bharata, and kings—the entire procession was wretched in separation from Rāma. Recounting the clusters of the Lord's virtues inwardly, everyone moved along the road in silence. After crossing the Yamunā they all reached the far bank; that day passed without food. They crossed the celestial river and made their second camp, where Rāma's friend Guha provided everyone excellent accommodation. Crossing the Saī, they bathed in the Gomatī and reached Ayodhyā on the fourth day. Janaka remained in the city for four days and put all the arrangements of state in order. Entrusting the kingdom to the ministers, guru, and Bharata, he prepared his company and departed for Tirhut. Following the guru's teaching, the city's women and men lived peacefully in Rāma's capital. Until Rāma's return, everyone undertook observances and fasts, gave up ornaments, enjoyments, and pleasures one after another, and lived upon hope in the appointed term.

Bharata instructed the ministers and faithful servants, assigning each one's work and firmly impressing his teaching. Then he called his younger brother, gave him counsel, and entrusted all service of the mothers to him. Summoning the brahmins, Bharata joined his hands, bowed, and appealed with words of humility: ‘For every task, high or low, good or bad, give your command without hesitation.’ He called relations, citizens, and subjects, reassured them, and settled them comfortably. With his younger brother he then went again to the guru's house, prostrated, joined his hands, and said: ‘If you command, may I remain under this observance?’ The sage's body thrilled with love as he answered: ‘Whatever you understand, say, and do will become the essence of duty in the world.’ Receiving instruction and a great blessing, Bharata summoned the astrologers and fixed the day. Without any rival claimant, he installed the Lord's sandals upon the throne.

Bowing his head at the feet of Rāma's mother and the guru, and receiving the command of the Lord's foot-seat, Bharata made a leaf hut at Nandigrāma. There the steadfast bearer of duty made his home. He wore matted hair and an ascetic's cloth, dug into the earth, and prepared a bed of kuśa grass. With love he observed the austere discipline of sages in food, clothing, utensils, vows, and rules. Abundant ornaments, garments, enjoyments, and pleasures he abandoned in body, mind, and speech as though they were three straws. Ayodhyā's kingdom made even Indra's realm envious, and hearing of Daśaratha's wealth put Kubera to shame. Yet Bharata lived in that city without attachment, like a bee in a garden of scentless campaka flowers. Devoted to Rāma, he rejected the sport of Fortune as a greatly blessed person rejects vomit. Bharata is an extraordinary vessel of love for Rāma, but not because of this conduct alone. The cātaka and swan are praised respectively for constancy and the wealth of discernment; Bharata possesses both.

Day by day Bharata's body grew leaner; its radiance, strength, and the beauty of his face diminished in the same measure. Yet his ever-new vow of love for Rāma grew full, the host of his virtues increased, and his mind never became stained. As an autumn lake shines when its water recedes, revealing reeds and blooming lotuses, so self-restraint, control of the senses, discipline, observance, and worship were stars in the stainless sky of Bharata's heart. Steady faith was the full moon of the appointed term, and remembrance of his master the radiant Milky Way. The moon of love for Rāma was fixed and faultless, shining ever brighter with its whole constellation. Bharata's way of life, understanding, and deeds—his devotion, detachment, virtues, and stainless glory—make even Śeṣa and Gaṇeśa, accomplished speakers all, hesitate to describe them; they are beyond the reach of speech. Each day Bharata lovingly worshiped the Lord's sandals, with a devotion his heart could not contain, and repeatedly sought their permission as he conducted the many affairs of state.
